user_input: What's the recommended way to target a button by the label a user would read on it?
reference: Reach for a role locator such as page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }). Playwright pushes you toward role-based locators because they mirror how real users and assistive tech experience the page.
reference_contexts: We recommend prioritizing role locators to locate elements, as it is the closest way to how users and assistive technology perceive the page.
llm_response:
The recommended way to target a button by the label a user would read on it is to use `page.getByRole()`. 

Documentation states that you should prioritize role locators because they are the closest way to how users and assistive technology perceive the page. When using `getByRole`, you should pass the accessible name (the label text) to pinpoint the exact element.

**Example:**
```javascript
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
```

You can also use a regular expression for the name to make the match case-insensitive:
```javascript
await page.getByRole('button', { name: /submit/i }).click();
```

user_input: If I don't configure anything, how long can a single test run before Playwright kills it, and what counts toward that budget?
reference: Each test gets 30 seconds out of the box, and that budget covers the test body plus fixture setup and any beforeEach hooks.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and beforeEach hooks is included in the test timeout.
llm_response:
If you do not configure anything, Playwright enforces a default timeout of 30 seconds for each test.

The following are included in this 30-second budget:
*   The test function itself.
*   Fixture setups.
*   `beforeEach` hooks.

Additionally, there is a separate timeout of the same value (30 seconds) that is shared between fixture teardowns and `afterEach` hooks, which applies after the test function has finished.

user_input: I have a flaky test I'd like re-run a couple of times on failure — what's the quickest command-line way?
reference: Pass a retry count on the run command, e.g. npx playwright test --retries=3 re-runs failing tests up to three times. Nothing is retried unless you opt in.
reference_contexts: Playwright supports test retries . When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.
llm_response:
The quickest command-line way to re-run a flaky test on failure is to use the `--retries` flag. You can specify the number of retry attempts as follows:

`npx playwright test --retries=N`

Replace `N` with the number of times you would like the test to be retried.
llm_references:
# Retries | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Test retries are a way to automatically re-run a test when it fails. This is useful when a test is flaky and fails intermittently. Test retries are configured in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

## Failures​ {#failures}

Playwright Test runs tests in worker processes. These processes are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

Consider the following snippet:


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe('suite',()=>{test.beforeAll(async()=>{/* ... */});test('first good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('second flaky',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('third good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test.afterAll(async()=>{/* ... */});});`


When
all tests pass
, they will run in order in the same worker process.

If you
enable
retries (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#retries)
, second worker process will start by retrying the failed test and continue from there.

Worker process #1 starts
`beforeAll`
hook runs
`first good`
passes
`second flaky`
fails
`afterAll`
hook runs
Worker process #2 starts
`beforeAll`
hook runs again
`second flaky`
is retried and passes
`third good`
passes
`afterAll`
hook runs

This scheme works perfectly for independent tests and guarantees that failing tests can't affect healthy ones.

## Retries​ {#retries}

Playwright supports
test retries
. When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.


`# Give failing tests 3 retry attemptsnpx playwrighttest--retries=3`


You can configure retries in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`# Give failing tests 3 retry attemptsnpx playwrighttest--retries=3`


You can configure retries in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Give failing tests 3 retry attemptsretries:3,});`


Playwright Test will categorize tests as follows:

"passed" - tests that passed on the first run;
"flaky" - tests that failed on the first run, but passed when retried;
"failed" - tests that failed on the first run and failed all retries.


`Running3tests using1worker✓ example.spec.ts:4:2 › first passes(438ms)x example.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky(691ms)✓ example.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky(522ms)✓ example.spec.ts:6:2 › third passes(932ms)1flakyexample.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky2passed(4s)`

user_input: I pulled a trace.zip off CI — how do I actually open it on my machine?
reference: Hand it to the CLI: npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip.
reference_contexts: npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip
llm_response:
You can open your `trace.zip` file using one of the following two methods:

### 1. Using the Playwright CLI (Recommended)
Run the following command in your terminal, replacing `path/to/trace.zip` with the actual path to your file:

`npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip`

### 2. Using the browser
You can use the web-based Trace Viewer at [trace.playwright.dev](https://trace.playwright.dev). Once on the site, you can open your trace by:
*   Dragging and dropping the `trace.zip` file into the browser window.
*   Clicking the **Select file** button to choose the file from your machine.

This tool processes the trace locally in your browser and does not transmit any data externally.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Trace Viewer is a GUI tool that helps you explore recorded Playwright traces after the script has run. Traces are a great way for debugging your tests when they fail on CI. You can open traces
locally (https://playwright.dev/docs/trace-viewer#opening-trace-viewer)
or in your browser on
trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev)
.

## Opening Trace Viewer​ {#opening-trace-viewer}

You can open a saved trace using either the Playwright CLI or in the browser at
trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev)
. Make sure to add the full path to where your
`trace.zip`
file is located.


`npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip`

## Recording a trace​ {#recording-a-trace}

### Tracing locally​ {#tracing-locally}

To record a trace during development mode set the
`--trace`
flag to
`on`
when running your tests. You can also use
UI Mode (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-ui-mode)
for a better developer experience, as it traces each test automatically.


`npx playwrighttest--traceon`


You can then open the HTML report and click on the trace icon to open the trace.


`npx playwright show-report`


### Tracing on CI​ {#tracing-on-ci}

Traces should be run on continuous integration on the first retry of a failed test by setting the
`trace: 'on-first-retry'`
option in the test configuration file. This will produce a
`trace.zip`
file for each test that was retried.

Test
Library
playwright.config.ts

`npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip`


### Usingtrace.playwright.dev​ {#using-traceplaywrightdev}

trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev)
is a statically hosted variant of the Trace Viewer. You can upload a trace file using drag and drop or via the
`Select file`
button.

Trace Viewer loads the trace entirely in your browser and does not transmit any data externally.

### Viewing remote traces​ {#viewing-remote-traces}

You can open remote traces directly using its URL. This makes it easy to view the remote trace without having to manually download the file from CI runs, for example.


`npx playwright show-trace https://example.com/trace.zip`


When using
trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev)
, you can also pass the URL of your uploaded trace at some accessible storage (e.g. inside your CI) as a query parameter. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) rules might apply.

Traces are recorded using the new
browserContext.tracing (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-tracing)
API:


`constbrowser=awaitchromium.launch();constcontext=awaitbrowser.newContext();// Start tracing before creating / navigating a page.awaitcontext.tracing.start({screenshots:true,snapshots:true});constpage=awaitcontext.newPage();awaitpage.goto('https://playwright.dev');// Stop tracing and export it into a zip archive.awaitcontext.tracing.stop({path:'trace.zip'});`


Traces are examined later with the Playwright CLI:


`npx playwright show-trace trace.zip`


That will open the following GUI:

👉 Read more in
trace viewer documentation (https://playwright.dev/docs/trace-viewer)
.

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({retries:process.env.CI?2:0,// set to 2 when running on CI// ...use:{trace:'on-first-retry',// record traces on first retry of each test},});`

user_input: How can I cap how many tests run in parallel straight from the command line?
reference: Bound the parallel worker count with the --workers flag, e.g. npx playwright test --workers 4.
reference_contexts: npx playwright test --workers 4
llm_response:
You can cap the number of parallel worker processes by using the `--workers` command line flag.

For example, to limit the number of workers to 4, use:
`npx playwright test --workers=4`

To disable parallelism by limiting the execution to a single worker, use:
`npx playwright test --workers=1`
llm_references:
Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

## Limit workers​ {#limit-workers}

You can control the maximum number of parallel worker processes via
command line (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-cli)
or in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

From the command line:


`npx playwrighttest--workers4`


In the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Limit the number of workers on CI, use default locallyworkers:process.env.CI?2:undefined,});`


## Disable parallelism​ {#disable-parallelism}

You can disable any parallelism by allowing just a single worker at any time. Either set
`workers: 1`
option in the configuration file or pass
`--workers=1`
to the command line.


`npx playwrighttest--workers=1`

`test.describe('runs in parallel with other describes',()=>{test.describe.configure({mode:'default'});test('in order 1',async({page})=>{});test('in order 2',async({page})=>{});});`


## Shard tests between multiple machines​ {#shard-tests-between-multiple-machines}

Playwright Test can shard a test suite, so that it can be executed on multiple machines. See
sharding guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-sharding)
for more details.


`npx playwrighttest--shard=2/3`


## Limit failures and fail fast​ {#limit-failures-and-fail-fast}

You can limit the number of failed tests in the whole test suite by setting
`maxFailures`
config option or passing
`--max-failures`
command line flag.

When running with "max failures" set, Playwright Test will stop after reaching this number of failed tests and skip any tests that were not executed yet. This is useful to avoid wasting resources on broken test suites.

Passing command line option:


`npx playwrighttest--max-failures=10`

# Running and debugging tests | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/running-tests>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

With Playwright you can run a single test, a set of tests, or all tests. Tests can be run on one browser or multiple browsers using the
`--project`
flag. Tests run in parallel by default and in headless mode, meaning no browser window opens while running the tests and results appear in the terminal. You can run tests in headed mode using the
`--headed`
CLI argument, or run your tests in
UI mode (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-ui-mode)
using the
`--ui`
flag to see a full trace of your tests.

You will learn

How to run tests from the command line (https://playwright.dev/docs/running-tests#command-line)
How to debug tests (https://playwright.dev/docs/running-tests#debugging-tests)
How to open the HTML test reporter (https://playwright.dev/docs/running-tests#test-reports)

## Running tests​ {#running-tests}

### Command line​ {#command-line}

# Parallelism | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test runs tests in parallel. In order to achieve that, it runs several worker processes that run at the same time. By default,
test files
are run in parallel. Tests in a single file are run in order, in the same worker process.

You can configure tests using
test.describe.configure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#parallelize-tests-in-a-single-file)
to run
tests in a single file
in parallel.
You can configure
entire project
to have all tests in all files to run in parallel using
testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
or
testConfig.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-fully-parallel)
.
To
disable
parallelism limit the number of
workers to one (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#disable-parallelism)
.

When you shard your tests, each shard can run on its own, utilizing the available CPU cores. This helps speed up the testing process by doing tasks simultaneously.

In a CI pipeline, each shard can run as a separate job, making use of the hardware resources available in your CI pipeline, like CPU cores, to run tests faster.

## Sharding tests between multiple machines​ {#sharding-tests-between-multiple-machines}

To shard the test suite, pass
`--shard=x/y`
to the command line. For example, to split the suite into four shards, each running one fourth of the tests:


`npx playwrighttest--shard=1/4npx playwrighttest--shard=2/4npx playwrighttest--shard=3/4npx playwrighttest--shard=4/4`


Now, if you run these shards in parallel on different jobs, your test suite completes four times faster.

`npx playwrighttest--workers=1`


## Parallelize tests in a single file​ {#parallelize-tests-in-a-single-file}

By default, tests in a single file are run in order. If you have many independent tests in a single file, you might want to run them in parallel with
test.describe.configure() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-configure)
.

Note that parallel tests are executed in separate worker processes and cannot share any state or global variables. Each test executes all relevant hooks just for itself, including
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
.


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe.configure({mode:'parallel'});test('runs in parallel 1',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('runs in parallel 2',async({page})=>{/* ... */});`


Alternatively, you can opt-in all tests into this fully-parallel mode in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({fullyParallel:true,});`

user_input: How do I choose an option in a <select>, and can I pick several at once?
reference: Call selectOption() with the option's value or label; pass an array when you need multiple selected.
reference_contexts: Selects one or multiple options in the <select> element with locator.selectOption() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-select-option) . You can specify option value , or label to select. Multiple options can be selected.
llm_response:
To choose an option in a `<select>` element, you use the `selectOption` method. You can match options by their value, label, or index.

### How to choose an option
You can pass a string (matching value or label) or an object (e.g., `{label: 'Blue'}`) to the method. Examples include:
*   **By value or label:** `page.selectOption('select#colors', 'blue');`
*   **By label specifically:** `page.selectOption('select#colors', {label: 'Blue'});`

### Can I pick several at once?
Yes, you can select multiple options by passing an array of values to the `selectOption` method. 

*   **Multiple selection:** `page.selectOption('select#colors', ['red', 'green', 'blue']);`

**Behavior notes:**
*   If the `<select>` element has the `multiple` attribute, all matching options provided in the array will be selected.
*   If the `<select>` element does not have the `multiple` attribute, only the first option matching one of the passed options will be selected.

user_input: If my page throws up an alert or confirm and I never handle it, will my test get stuck?
reference: No — with no dialog listener registered, Playwright dismisses dialogs automatically, so they won't block the run.
reference_contexts: If there is no listener for page.on('dialog') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-dialog) , all dialogs are automatically dismissed.
llm_response:
No, your test will not get stuck if you do not handle the dialog. By default, Playwright automatically dismisses dialogs when no `page.on('dialog')` or `browserContext.on('dialog')` listeners are present.

However, if you do register a listener for the `'dialog'` event, you **must** call either `dialog.accept()` or `dialog.dismiss()`. If you register a listener but fail to perform one of these actions (for example, if you only log the message), the page will freeze waiting for the dialog, and subsequent actions like `locator.click()` will stall and never finish.

note
Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.

Here is the simplest way to handle the file download:


`// Start waiting for download before clicking. Note no await.constdownloadPromise=page.waitForEvent('download');awaitpage.getByText('Download file').click();constdownload=awaitdownloadPromise;// Wait for the download process to complete and save the downloaded file somewhere.awaitdownload.saveAs('/path/to/save/at/'+download.suggestedFilename());`

If you have no idea what initiates the download, you can still handle the event:


`page.on('download',download=>download.path().then(console.log));`


Note that handling the event forks the control flow and makes the script harder to follow. Your scenario might end while you are downloading a file since your main control flow is not awaiting for this operation to resolve.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

For every attachment downloaded by the page,
page.on('download') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-download)
event is emitted. All these attachments are downloaded into a temporary folder. You can obtain the download url, file name and payload stream using the

You should store saved login state in a directory named `playwright/.auth`.

To keep this state out of version control, you must add the `playwright/.auth` directory to your `.gitignore` file. This is the
recommended

without server-side state
. Authenticate once in the

# Authentication | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/auth>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright executes tests in isolated environments called
browser contexts (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures. Tests can load existing authenticated state. This eliminates the need to authenticate in every test and speeds up test execution.

## Core concepts​ {#core-concepts}

Regardless of the authentication strategy you choose, you are likely to store authenticated browser state on the file system.

We recommend to create
`playwright/.auth`
directory and add it to your
`.gitignore`
. Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file in this
`playwright/.auth`
directory. Later on, tests will reuse this state and start already authenticated.

Storage state is interchangeable between
BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext)
and
APIRequestContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-apirequestcontext)
. You can use it to log in via API calls and then create a new context with cookies already there. The following code snippet retrieves state from an authenticated
APIRequestContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-apirequestcontext)
and creates a new
BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext)
with that state.


`constrequestContext=awaitrequest.newContext({httpCredentials:{username:'user',password:'passwd'}});awaitrequestContext.get(`https://api.example.com/login`);// Save storage state into the file.awaitrequestContext.storageState({path:'state.json'});// Create a new context with the saved storage state.constcontext=awaitbrowser.newContext({storageState:'state.json'});`

## Running tests​ {#running-tests}

### Command line​ {#command-line}

You can run your tests with the
`playwright test`
command. This runs your tests on all browsers as configured in the
`playwright.config`
file, and results appear in the terminal. Tests run in headless mode by default, meaning no browser window opens while running the tests.


`npx playwrighttest`


### Run tests in UI mode​ {#run-tests-in-ui-mode}

We highly recommend running your tests with
UI Mode (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-ui-mode)
for a better developer experience where you can easily walk through each step of the test and visually see what was happening before, during and after each step. UI mode also comes with many other features such as the locator picker, watch mode and more.


`npx playwrighttest--ui`


Check out our
detailed guide on UI Mode (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-ui-mode)
to learn more about its features.

### Run tests in headed mode​ {#run-tests-in-headed-mode}

Check out our
detailed guide on UI Mode (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-ui-mode)
to learn more about its features.

### Run tests in headed mode​ {#run-tests-in-headed-mode}

To run your tests in headed mode, use the
`--headed`
flag. This gives you the ability to visually see how Playwright interacts with the website.


`npx playwrighttest--headed`


### Run tests on different browsers​ {#run-tests-on-different-browsers}

To specify which browser you would like to run your tests on, use the
`--project`
flag followed by the browser name.


`npx playwrighttest--projectwebkit`


To specify multiple browsers to run your tests on, use the
`--project`
flag multiple times followed by each browser name.


`npx playwrighttest--projectwebkit--projectfirefox`


### Run specific tests​ {#run-specific-tests}

To run a single test file, pass in the test file name that you want to run.


`npx playwrighttestlanding-page.spec.ts`

user_input: How do I split my tests to run across several machines at once?
reference: Shard with --shard=x/y — run 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 on four machines so each takes a quarter of the suite.
reference_contexts:
npx playwright test --shard=1/4
npx playwright test --shard=2/4
npx playwright test --shard=3/4
npx playwright test --shard=4/4
llm_response:
To split your tests to run across several machines, you use sharding. Sharding allows you to divide your test suite into smaller parts (shards) that can run independently on different machines or CI jobs.

### How to shard tests
To shard your test suite, pass the `--shard=x/y` flag to the command line, where `x` is the current shard index and `y` is the total number of shards.

For example, to split your suite into four shards, run these commands on four separate machines or CI jobs:
* `npx playwright test --shard=1/4`
* `npx playwright test --shard=2/4`
* `npx playwright test --shard=3/4`
* `npx playwright test --shard=4/4`

### Reporting
When sharding across multiple machines, it is recommended to use the 'blob' reporter in your `playwright.config.ts` to facilitate merging results later:

```typescript
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
export default defineConfig({
  reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',
});
```

After the shards complete, you can merge the resulting reports into a single report using the merge-reports CLI:
`npx playwright merge-reports path/to/blob-reports-dir`

You can also specify the output format for the merged report, for example:
`npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports`

# Sharding | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-sharding>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

By default, Playwright runs test files in
parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
and strives for optimal utilization of CPU cores on your machine. In order to achieve even greater parallelisation, you can further scale Playwright test execution by running tests on multiple machines simultaneously. We call this mode of operation "sharding". Sharding in Playwright means splitting your tests into smaller parts called "shards". Each shard is like a separate job that can run independently. The whole purpose is to divide your tests to speed up test runtime.

When you shard your tests, each shard can run on its own, utilizing the available CPU cores. This helps speed up the testing process by doing tasks simultaneously.

When you shard your tests, each shard can run on its own, utilizing the available CPU cores. This helps speed up the testing process by doing tasks simultaneously.

In a CI pipeline, each shard can run as a separate job, making use of the hardware resources available in your CI pipeline, like CPU cores, to run tests faster.

## Sharding tests between multiple machines​ {#sharding-tests-between-multiple-machines}

To shard the test suite, pass
`--shard=x/y`
to the command line. For example, to split the suite into four shards, each running one fourth of the tests:


`npx playwrighttest--shard=1/4npx playwrighttest--shard=2/4npx playwrighttest--shard=3/4npx playwrighttest--shard=4/4`


Now, if you run these shards in parallel on different jobs, your test suite completes four times faster.

## Merging reports from multiple environments​ {#merging-reports-from-multiple-environments}

If you want to run the same tests in multiple environments, as opposed to shard your tests onto multiple machines, you need to differentiate these environments.

In this case, it is useful to specify the
testConfig.tag (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-tag)
property, to tag all tests with the environment name. This tag will be automatically picked up by the blob report and later on by the merge tool.

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({reporter:process.env.CI?'blob':'html',tag:process.env.CI_ENVIRONMENT_NAME,// for example "@APIv2"});`


## Merge-reports CLI​ {#merge-reports-cli}

`npx playwright merge-reports path/to/blob-reports-dir`
reads all blob reports from the passed directory and merges them into a single report.

`# Install NPM packagesnpmci# Install Playwright browsers and dependenciesnpx playwrightinstall--with-deps`

Run your tests

`npx playwrighttest`


## Workers​ {#workers}

We recommend setting
workers (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-workers)
to "1" in CI environments to prioritize stability and reproducibility. Running tests sequentially ensures each test gets the full system resources, avoiding potential conflicts. However, if you have a powerful self-hosted CI system, you may enable
parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
tests. For wider parallelization, consider
sharding (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#shard-tests-between-multiple-machines)
- distributing tests across multiple CI jobs.

`test.describe('runs in parallel with other describes',()=>{test.describe.configure({mode:'default'});test('in order 1',async({page})=>{});test('in order 2',async({page})=>{});});`


## Shard tests between multiple machines​ {#shard-tests-between-multiple-machines}

Playwright Test can shard a test suite, so that it can be executed on multiple machines. See

## Limit failures and fail fast​ {#limit-failures-and-fail-fast}

You can limit the number of failed tests in the whole test suite by setting
`maxFailures`
config option or passing
`--max-failures`
command line flag.

When running with "max failures" set, Playwright Test will stop after reaching this number of failed tests and skip any tests that were not executed yet. This is useful to avoid wasting resources on broken test suites.

Passing command line option:


`npx playwrighttest--max-failures=10`

`npx playwright merge-reports--reporterhtml ./all-blob-reports`


This will produce a standard HTML report into
`playwright-report`
directory.

## GitHub Actions example​ {#github-actions-example}

GitHub Actions supports
sharding tests between multiple jobs (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-jobs/using-a-matrix-for-your-jobs)
using the
jobs.<job_id>.strategy.matrix (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions#jobsjob_idstrategymatrix)
option. The
`matrix`

`reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',`

user_input: How do I watch the browser as my script runs and slow it down enough to follow along?
reference: Launch non-headless and pace each step with slowMo — e.g. chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 }).
reference_contexts:
// Chromium, Firefox, or WebKit
await chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 });
llm_response:
To watch the browser as your script runs and slow it down, you should use the following approaches:

**1. To watch the browser (Headed mode):**
*   **For scripts:** Use the `headless: false` launch option.
    ```javascript
    await chromium.launch({ headless: false });
    ```
*   **For tests:** Enable the **Show Browser** option in the Playwright sidebar.

**2. To slow down execution:**
Use the `slowMo` option, which slows down Playwright operations by a specified number of milliseconds.
```javascript
await chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 });
```

Note that for WebKit, launching the WebKit Inspector during execution will prevent the script from executing further and will reset pre-configured user agent and device emulation.

user_input: Two problems with how our team writes tests. The recorder is the fastest way for people to get started, but the selectors it emits break on the next refactor, and half our app is behind a login so recording anything past the sign-in page means clicking through the form by hand every single time. Are both of these things the recorder can be told to handle?
reference: Both are, and they're separate mechanisms. On selectors: the generator isn't emitting raw CSS by accident — it inspects the page and picks what it judges the best locator, prioritising role, text and test id locators in that order, and when a candidate matches several elements it refines it until it uniquely identifies the target. So brittle output is usually a signal about the markup rather than the tool: give the elements you care about a test id (or accessible roles and names) and the recorder will prefer those. You can also use Pick Locator to grab and hand-tune a single locator rather than recording a whole flow. On the login: record the authentication once with `npx playwright codegen <url> --save-storage=auth.json`, which writes the cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB state at the end of the session, then start every later recording with `npx playwright codegen --load-storage=auth.json <url>`, which restores that state so the app comes up already signed in and you record only the part you care about. That saved state is the same kind of artifact your suite consumes as storageState, so the recorded flow and the running tests can share it.
reference_contexts: Playwright will look at your page and figure out the best locator, prioritizing role, text and test id locators. If the generator finds multiple elements matching the locator, it will improve the locator to make it resilient that uniquely identifies the target element.
The test generator can also generate a test while preserving authenticated state.

Run codegen with --save-storage to save cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB data at the end of the session. This is useful to separately record an authentication step and reuse it later when recording more tests.

Run with --load-storage to consume the previously loaded storage from the auth.json. This way, all cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB data will be restored, bringing most web apps to the authenticated state without the need to login again. This means you can continue generating tests from the logged in state.
You can generate locators with the test generator.
llm_response:
The recorder cannot be told to handle these issues directly through settings, but the documentation provides specific ways to address both:

*   **Resilient Locators:** The test generator is designed to prioritize role, text, and test id locators. If it finds multiple elements matching a locator, it will improve the locator to make it resilient and uniquely identify the target element. You can also use the "Pick locator" tool to have Playwright determine the best locator for any element.
*   **Login/Authentication:** You do not need to record the login form every time. Instead, you should use **project dependencies** to define a setup test that performs the login once. This allows you to reuse the authenticated state across multiple tests without having to log in again for each one. 

Additionally, if you need to use a non-standard setup for recording, you can use `page.pause()` to open a window with codegen controls, or use the `--user-data-dir` flag with `npx playwright codegen` to persist browser data.

user_input: When I shard across CI jobs, how do workers, fullyParallel and retries interact to keep runs balanced and reliable?
reference: Inside each shard Playwright still runs worker processes; turning on fullyParallel shards at the individual-test level so each job gets an even slice rather than whole files. Keep retries enabled so that when a worker is torn down after a failure it simply restarts and re-runs the affected test.
reference_contexts: When fullyParallel: true is enabled, Playwright Test runs individual tests in parallel across multiple shards, ensuring each shard receives an even distribution of tests. This allows for test-level granularity, meaning each shard will attempt to balance the number of individual tests it runs.
Workers are always shutdown after a test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures) to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.
If you enable retries , second worker process will start by retrying the failed test and continue from there.
llm_response:
To keep runs balanced and reliable when sharding across CI jobs, the interaction between `fullyParallel`, workers, and sharding functions as follows:

### Balancing Shards
*   **`fullyParallel: true` (Recommended):** This is the preferred mode for balanced distribution. Tests are split at the individual test level, allowing Playwright to optimize and ensure an even distribution of tests across shards.
*   **`fullyParallel: false` (Default):** Tests are split at the file level. To maintain balance in this mode, you must manually organize your test files to ensure they are small and evenly sized.

### Workers and Reliability
*   **Recommendation:** It is recommended to set `workers` to `1` in CI environments to prioritize stability and reproducibility, as this ensures each test receives full system resources and avoids potential conflicts.
*   **Alternative:** If you have a powerful self-hosted CI system, you may enable parallel tests by adjusting the `workers` setting, though this is secondary to the recommendation of using sharding for wider parallelization across multiple machines.

### Retries
The provided documentation does not contain information regarding how `retries` interact with sharding, `fullyParallel`, or workers to keep runs balanced and reliable.

user_input: Should I use a globalSetup file or project dependencies for one-time setup, and why?
reference: Prefer project dependencies. Because a dependency is a real project that runs ahead of the others, it plugs into the runner properly — the setup shows up in the HTML report, is traced, and can use fixtures — whereas globalSetup misses some of that.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach, as it integrates better with the Playwright test runner: your HTML report will include the global setup, traces will be recorded, and fixtures can be used.

Dependencies are a list of projects that need to run before the tests in another project run. They can be useful for configuring the global setup actions so that one project depends on this running first.
llm_response:
You should use **project dependencies**, as this is the recommended approach.

Project dependencies are preferred because they integrate better with the Playwright test runner, providing the following advantages over the `globalSetup` config option:

*   **Reporting and Debugging:** Setup is shown as a separate project in the HTML report, and full trace recording is supported.
*   **Fixtures:** Playwright fixtures are fully supported within setup.
*   **Browser Management:** You can manage browsers via the `browser` fixture, whereas `globalSetup` requires manual management via `browserType.launch()`.
*   **Configuration:** Standard config options (such as `headless` or `testIdAttribute`) are automatically applied, and parallelism and retries are supported.

In contrast, the `globalSetup` config option does not support trace recording, fixtures, or automatic application of config options, and it is not shown in the HTML report. The documentation explicitly advises considering project dependencies instead to get full feature support.

user_input: Our app registers a service worker for offline support. Every route handler I install works fine against a build with the worker disabled, but against the real build some requests reach the network untouched while others are intercepted, and which is which seems to change between runs. What decides whether a request is interceptable here, and what's the sane way to test against this app?
reference: Whether a request is routable depends on who owns it. Once a service worker with a fetch handler is installed it sits between the page and the network: the page-owned request is served by the worker and never reaches the network, so it isn't routable, while the worker's own outbound request is a separate, service-worker-owned request that context routing does see. That split is why interception looks inconsistent — you're catching some requests at one layer and missing others at the other, and which layer serves a given resource depends on the worker's cache state, hence the run-to-run variation. If you're doing ordinary network mocking, the documented answer is not to reason about this at all: set `serviceWorkers: 'block'` in the config's `use` options so the worker never registers and everything is page-owned and routable. Only if you specifically need to assert on the worker's own traffic should you leave them enabled and branch inside the handler on `route.request().serviceWorker()` — noting that calling .frame() on such a request throws, and that requests for updated worker scripts cannot currently be routed at all.
reference_contexts: If you're looking to do general network mocking, routing, and interception, please see the Network Guide first. Playwright provides built-in APIs for this use case that don't require the information below. However, if you're interested in requests made by Service Workers themselves, please read below.
To disable service workers, set testOptions.serviceWorkers to 'block'.

Only the Service Worker-owned request for the resource was routable via browserContext.route(); the Frame-owned events for data.json are not routeable, as they would not have even had the possibility to hit the external network since the Service Worker has a fetch handler registered.

user_input: Our GitHub Actions job installs cleanly — `npm ci` is green — and then every test fails at browser launch complaining about missing shared libraries. It's an ubuntu-latest runner, and the identical commit runs fine on all three of our developers' machines. What is the CI box missing that a laptop already has, and what's the durable way to fix it?
reference: Installing the npm package is not the same as provisioning a machine that can run browsers, and that's the gap. `npm ci` fetches the library; the browser binaries are downloaded separately, and those binaries need operating-system level libraries that a developer machine already has from everyday browser use and a bare Linux runner does not. So there are two things to install, and the combined step is `npx playwright install --with-deps`, which fetches the browsers and the OS dependencies together — that's exactly the step the recommended GitHub Actions workflow runs between `npm ci` and the test command. The alternative, and the more durable one if you also do visual comparison, is to run the job inside the official container image via `jobs.<job_id>.container`: it keeps the dependencies out of the host environment and gives you a consistent rendering environment, which matters because screenshots differ across platforms.

user_input: Almost all of our tests stub the search endpoint so they're hermetic, and that's been great until the backend quietly renamed a field and every test stayed green while production broke. I want to keep most tests stubbed but have a couple that exercise the real endpoint and only override one flag in whatever comes back. Can the same interception mechanism do both, and what changes between them?
reference: Both go through the same route handler; what differs is whether you ever let the request reach the network. A hermetic stub never does: page.route(url, route => route.fulfill({ json: ... })) answers from the test and the server is never contacted, which is why a server-side shape change can't fail it. To modify a real response you have to fetch it first — inside the handler call `const response = await route.fetch()`, read the real body with `await response.json()`, mutate the field you care about, and then fulfill with the edited payload: `await route.fulfill({ response, json })`. That gives you the real contract for everything you didn't touch, so the renamed field would have surfaced. Routes are matched most-recently-registered first and are scoped to the page or context they were registered on, so a spec-level `page.route` override can sit on top of a project-wide stub. If you want the real traffic recorded once and replayed thereafter, that's what HAR replay is for.
reference_contexts: Mock API requests: All the requests made by the page, including XHRs and fetch requests, can be tracked, modified and mocked.

Yes, the same interception mechanism can be used for both stubbing and modifying real responses by combining API Testing with request interception.

To achieve this, you use response interception. The difference between the two approaches is how you handle the response data:

*   **For stubbing:** You intercept the request and provide a full mock response.
*   **For exercising the real endpoint with a modification:** You perform the request to the real endpoint (using the `request` fixture) and then use response interception to modify the specific flag in the returned data before it reaches the page.

The documentation notes that response interception is achieved by combining API Testing with request interception.

user_input: How does device emulation (viewport, user agent, touch) get applied per test, and why doesn't it bleed into other tests?
reference: Device parameters come from Playwright's device registry and are applied at the browser-context level. Since every test runs in its own isolated context — which can also carry mobile emulation, permissions, locale and color scheme — the emulation stays scoped to that test.
reference_contexts: Playwright comes with a registry of device parameters (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json) using playwright.devices (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-playwright#playwright-devices) for selected desktop, tablet and mobile devices. It can be used to simulate browser behavior for a specific device such as user agent, screen size, viewport and if it has touch enabled. All tests will run with the specified device parameters.

Browser contexts can also be used to emulate multi-page scenarios involving mobile devices, permissions, locale and color scheme. Check out our Emulation (https://playwright.dev/docs/emulation) guide for more details.
llm_response:
Device emulation is applied per test or per project by configuring the `use` property. It does not bleed into other tests because Playwright creates isolated browser contexts for each test.

### How it is applied
You can apply emulation settings (such as `viewport`, `userAgent`, `hasTouch`, `colorScheme`, etc.) using the following methods:

*   **Per Project:** In `playwright.config.ts`, define projects with specific `use` configurations. You can use the built-in `devices` registry to apply presets:
    ```typescript
    projects: [
      {
        name: 'Mobile Safari',
        use: { ...devices['iPhone 13'] },
      },
    ]
    ```
*   **Global Default:** Set emulation options in the `use` object within the top-level `defineConfig` in `playwright.config.ts`.
*   **Per Test:** Use `test.use()` within a test file to override settings for that specific test:
    ```typescript
    test.use({ colorScheme: 'dark' });
    test('my test', async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ });
    ```
*   **Manual Context/Page Creation:** When using the library directly, you can pass emulation parameters when creating a new context or page:
    ```typescript
    const context = await browser.newContext({ ...iphone13 });
    const page = await browser.newPage({ colorScheme: 'dark' });
    ```

### Why it doesn't bleed
Emulation settings are applied to specific browser contexts. Because Playwright executes tests in isolated contexts, settings defined for one test or project do not affect others. Projects represent distinct browser configurations, and each test runs within its own isolated environment, ensuring consistency and preventing configuration leakage.

user_input: One fixture is slow, but I don't want to inflate every test's timeout. How do fixture and test timeouts relate, and what's the fix?
reference: A fixture's setup counts against the test's clock, so a sluggish one can trip test timeouts. Hand that fixture its own longer timeout through the tuple option and leave the test's timeout tight.
reference_contexts: By default, fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures) shares timeout with the test. However, for slow fixtures, especially worker-scoped (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#worker-scoped-fixtures) ones, it is convenient to have a separate timeout. This way you can keep the overall test timeout small, and give the slow fixture more time.

Fixture is considered to be a part of a test, and so its setup and teardown running time counts towards the test timeout. Therefore, a slow fixture may cause test timeouts. You can set a separate larger timeout for such a fixture, and keep the overall test timeout small.

user_input: Our CI machines are a lot slower than our laptops and I've been sprinkling per-assertion timeouts around to get the suite green, which is clearly the wrong shape. Some tests now fail with a message about the test itself rather than the assertion, and raising the assertion timeout further doesn't help those at all. How many separate budgets am I actually dealing with, and which one do I raise?
reference: Three budgets, nested, which is why raising the wrong one does nothing. The test timeout is 30 seconds by default and covers the whole test — the test function plus fixture setup plus beforeEach hooks — and it's what you're hitting when the failure names the test rather than an assertion; raise it in the config's `timeout`, or per test with test.setTimeout(120_000), or test.slow() to triple the default. Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have their own separate 5-second expect timeout, which is unrelated to the test timeout and is the one reported in a 'expect.toHaveText with timeout 5000ms' call log; set it globally with `expect: { timeout: 10_000 }` or per assertion with a { timeout } option. Because the assertion budget is consumed inside the test budget, pushing the expect timeout above the test timeout accomplishes nothing — the test dies first. beforeAll/afterAll get their own timeout, equal to the test timeout by default and adjustable inside the hook. export default defineConfig({ expect: { timeout: 10_000, }, });

beforeAll and afterAll hooks have a separate timeout, by default equal to test timeout. You can change it separately for each hook by calling testInfo.setTimeout() inside the hook.
llm_response:
You are dealing with three separate budgets:

1.  **Assertion timeout:** This applies to auto-retrying assertions (e.g., `expect(locator).toHaveText()`). It is unrelated to the test timeout and defaults to 5 seconds.
2.  **Test timeout:** This is the budget for the individual test itself. When a test fails with a message about the test rather than the assertion, it is because this budget has been exceeded. You can adjust this using `testInfo.setTimeout()`.
3.  **Global timeout:** This is the budget for the entire test suite run. It is set in the config via `globalTimeout`.

**Which one to raise:**
Since you stated that raising the assertion timeout does not help with tests that fail with a message about the test itself, you should raise the **test timeout** using `testInfo.setTimeout()`.

reference: Filter the parent by the child locator — e.g. getByRole('listitem').filter({ has: child }) — which is evaluated relative to the parent match. xpath=.. works but is brittle: any DOM change can break it, so prefer filtering.
reference_contexts: The filtering locator must be relative to the original locator and is queried starting with the original locator match, not the document root.

The reliable way to select a parent row based on a child element is to use `locator.filter()` with the `has` option.

**Example:**

You should avoid `xpath=..` because it is not reliable; any changes to the DOM structure will break your tests. XPath locators are tied to the implementation and the DOM structure, making them prone to failure when the page changes. `locator.filter()` is preferred because it is more resilient.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Large test suites can be structured to optimize ease of authoring and maintenance. Page object models are one such approach to structure your test suite.

A page object represents a part of your web application. An e-commerce web application might have a home page, a listings page and a checkout page. Each of them can be represented by page object models.

simplify maintenance

llm_response:
Before performing a `locator.click()`, Playwright verifies the following actionability checks:

*   The locator resolves to exactly one element.
*   The element is visible.
*   The element is stable (not animating or has completed animation).
*   The element receives events (is not obscured by other elements).
*   The element is enabled.

These checks relate to the "auto-waiting" performed by a plain click because Playwright automatically waits for all of these relevant conditions to pass before executing the action. If these checks do not pass within the specified `timeout`, the action fails with a `TimeoutError`. This auto-waiting mechanism ensures the action behaves as expected without the need for manual waits.

user_input: Where do downloaded files go, and why might they disappear before I can use them?
reference: Downloaded files sit in a temporary folder and belong to whichever context fetched them, so they vanish the instant that context is torn down. Each test gets a freshly created context, so grab anything you need before the test ends.
reference_contexts: Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.
Playwright uses browser contexts to achieve Test Isolation. Each test has its own Browser Context. Running the test creates a new browser context each time.
llm_response:
Downloaded files are stored in a temporary directory by default. You can specify a custom directory for these files by using the `downloadsPath` option in `browserType.launch()`.

Files may disappear before you can use them for the following reasons:

*   **Browser Context Closure:** Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.
*   **Temporary Directory Cleanup:** If a `downloadsPath` is not specified, the default temporary directory is deleted when the browser closes.
*   **Control Flow Issues:** If you handle the download event using `page.on('download', ...)` without awaiting the operation, your script may finish and close the browser context while the download is still in progress.

To ensure you can use the files, you should use `download.saveAs()` to save the file to a permanent location, or ensure your script properly awaits the download process.

user_input: We rolled our own visual checks: capture a PNG, compare it byte-for-byte with a committed file, fail on any difference. It's unusable — it fails on the first run of any new test, it fails constantly on CI with what look like anti-aliasing differences, and there's no way to accept a legitimate design change short of regenerating files by hand. What does the built-in comparison do differently at each of those three points?
reference: Each of your three problems is a thing the built-in assertion already handles, because capturing an image and asserting on one are different operations. page.screenshot() just returns a buffer; expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() is a full comparison assertion. On first run there is no baseline, so instead of failing meaninglessly it takes screenshots until two consecutive ones match — which also settles animation and rendering noise — saves the result as the reference and reports that it wrote it; you commit that file. On CI, the baseline is keyed by environment: the snapshot name like example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png encodes the browser and platform (the project name replaces the browser when you use multiple projects) precisely because rendering, fonts and anti-aliasing differ across platforms, so Linux CI compares against its own baseline rather than your macOS one. And byte-exactness isn't required: `maxDiffPixels` (per assertion or globally under `expect: { toHaveScreenshot: ... }`) sets an allowance. When a change is intentional you re-baseline with `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` rather than editing files.

The built-in `toHaveScreenshot()` comparison addresses your three issues as follows:

*   **Failing on the first run:** Instead of requiring a pre-committed file, Playwright automatically generates reference screenshots on the first execution.
*   **Failing on CI due to minor differences (e.g., anti-aliasing):** Unlike a byte-for-byte comparison, Playwright allows for configurable tolerance. You can use the `threshold` option (to configure the acceptable color difference) or the `maxDiffPixels` option (to allow a specific number of pixels to differ) to prevent tests from failing due to minor rendering variations. These can be set per-test or globally in `playwright.config.ts`.
*   **Accepting legitimate design changes:** The documentation does not explicitly detail the workflow for updating snapshots, but it notes that Playwright generates reference screenshots automatically on the first run and provides mechanisms to compare against those references in subsequent runs.

user_input: We added an automated accessibility scan to the suite and it's been green for months. This sprint a screen-reader user reported that our settings panel now reads its sections in the wrong order after a refactor that only moved markup around — and the scan didn't say a word about it. What class of problem is that scan actually able to catch, what would have caught the regression, and can both live in the same test?
reference: The scan and the regression are aimed at different things, which is why one sailed past the other. An automated scan — the documented approach uses the @axe-core/playwright package, where you await `new AxeBuilder({ page }).analyze()` and assert the returned `violations` array is empty — detects *rule* violations such as missing or invalid properties. It has no opinion about whether the structure is the one you intended, and the docs are explicit that many accessibility problems can only be found through manual testing, recommending a combination of automated scans, manual assessment and inclusive user testing. What your refactor changed was the shape of the accessibility tree, and that is what an aria snapshot pins: expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot() captures a YAML representation of the accessibility tree — the hierarchy of accessible elements with their roles, attributes, values and text, with indentation carrying the nesting — and fails when the current tree stops matching it. Order and nesting are part of that representation, so a moved section shows as a diff. The two compose: accessibility tests are ordinary tests, so you can put both in one spec or keep separate ones. Bear in mind the tradeoff the docs draw between the styles — targeted assertions check one specific condition and get verbose over complex structures, while snapshots capture whole-structure state and are best for outputs that rarely change shape, which also means they need deliberate re-baselining when a change is intentional.
reference_contexts: The following examples rely on the @axe-core/playwright package which adds support for running the axe accessibility testing engine as part of your Playwright tests.

Automated accessibility tests can detect some common accessibility problems such as missing or invalid properties. But many accessibility problems can only be discovered through manual testing. We recommend using a combination of automated testing, manual accessibility assessments, and inclusive user testing.
Accessibility tests work just like any other Playwright test. You can either create separate test cases for them, or integrate accessibility scans and assertions into your existing test cases.

In Playwright, aria snapshots provide a YAML representation of the accessibility tree of a page. These snapshots can be stored and compared later to verify if the page structure remains consistent or meets defined expectations.

The YAML format describes the hierarchical structure of accessible elements on the page, detailing roles, attributes, values, and text content. The structure follows a tree-like syntax, where each node represents an accessible element, and indentation indicates nested elements.
Snapshot testing is ideal for: UI testing of whole pages and components. Broad structural checks for complex UI components. Regression testing for outputs that rarely change structure.
llm_response:
The automated accessibility scan is able to catch common accessibility problems such as missing or invalid properties, including:
*   Text with poor color contrast.
*   UI controls and form elements missing labels.
*   Interactive elements with duplicate IDs.

The regression you described—a screen-reader user experiencing an incorrect reading order—is a problem that cannot be detected by automated testing. Many accessibility problems can only be discovered through manual testing. For manual assessments, the documentation recommends using Accessibility Insights for Web.

Both automated and manual testing can live in the same test suite. You can either create separate test cases for accessibility scans or integrate them into your existing test cases.

## Handling known issues​ {#handling-known-issues}

A common question when adding accessibility tests to an application is "how do I suppress known violations?" The following examples demonstrate a few techniques you can use.

### Excluding individual elements from a scan​ {#excluding-individual-elements-from-a-scan}

You can constrain an accessibility scan to only run those rules which are "tagged" as corresponding to specific WCAG success criteria by using
AxeBuilder.withTags() (https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core-npm/blob/develop/packages/playwright/README.md#axebuilderwithtagstags-stringarray)
. For example,
Accessibility Insights for Web's Automated Checks (https://accessibilityinsights.io/docs/web/getstarted/fastpass/?referrer=playwright-accessibility-testing-js)
only include axe rules that test for violations of WCAG A and AA success criteria; to match that behavior, you would use the tags
`wcag2a`
,
`wcag2aa`
,
`wcag21a`
, and
`wcag21aa`
.

Note that automated testing cannot detect all types of WCAG violations.

Here is an example of excluding one element from being scanned in one specific test:


`test('should not have any accessibility violations outside of elements with known issues',async({page,})=>{awaitpage.goto('https://your-site.com/page-with-known-issues');constaccessibilityScanResults=awaitnewAxeBuilder({page}).exclude('#element-with-known-issue').analyze();expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations).toEqual([]);});`


If the element in question is used repeatedly in many pages, consider
using a test fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/accessibility-testing#using-a-test-fixture-for-common-axe-configuration)
to reuse the same
`AxeBuilder`
configuration across multiple tests.

user_input: I need to assert that every row in our pricing table renders right-aligned, which isn't in the DOM anywhere — it's a computed style. Nothing on the locator exposes it, and my first attempt at reaching into the page came back with undefined for the threshold I was comparing against, even though it's a plain number defined right above the call.
reference: Two boundaries are in play. First, to get at computed style you have to run code in the page: a locator resolves to elements but only exposes what the API models, so anything the API doesn't cover you obtain with evaluate. For the whole set at once use locator.evaluateAll(), whose callback receives the array of matching elements — e.g. `await page.locator('td.price').evaluateAll(els => els.map(e => getComputedStyle(e).textAlign))` — returning an ordinary array back into the test. Second, that callback executes in the browser, in a different context from your test file, so it cannot close over test variables; that's why your threshold was undefined rather than throwing at definition. Pass it explicitly as the second argument: `locator.evaluateAll((els, limit) => ..., limit)`. Whatever you return has to be serializable to cross back — return the strings or numbers you want to assert on, not DOM nodes.
reference_contexts: The code inside locator.evaluateAll() runs in the page, you can call any DOM apis there.
const rows = page.getByRole('listitem'); const texts = await rows.evaluateAll( list => list.map(element => element.textContent));

Evaluated scripts run in the browser environment, while your test runs in a testing environments. This means you cannot use variables from your test in the page and vice versa. Instead, you should pass them explicitly as an argument.
llm_response:
To assert that every row in your pricing table renders with a right-aligned computed style, use the `toHaveCSS` assertion. This assertion is designed to resolve a locator to an element and verify its computed CSS style [2].

You can implement this by iterating over the rows and applying the assertion:

```javascript
const rows = page.locator('tr'); // Adjust selector to target your specific pricing table rows
for (const row of await rows.all()) {
  await expect(row).toHaveCSS('text-align', 'right');
}
```

**Key details:**
*   **`toHaveCSS`**: This is the specific method for checking computed styles [2].
*   **Options**: If you need to adjust the retry duration for the assertion, you can pass a `timeout` option (in milliseconds) [1].
*   **Pseudo-elements**: If the alignment is applied to a pseudo-element, you can specify it using the `pseudo` option [1].

user_input: I want to parameterize the same tests with different values — both at the test level and across environments. How do these two levels differ?
reference: You can parameterize at the test level or the project level. Project-level parameterization uses option fixtures whose values you set in each project's config, which is how you run the same tests against different environments.
reference_contexts: You can either parameterize tests on a test level or on a project level.

Playwright Test supports running multiple test projects that can be configured separately. You can use "option" fixtures to make your configuration options declarative and type safe. Learn more about parameterizing tests (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parameterize) .
llm_response:
Test-level parameterization and project-level parameterization differ in their implementation and scope:

**Test-level parameterization**
*   **Implementation:** You use a `forEach` loop to iterate over an array of data, calling `test()` or `test.describe()` inside the loop to generate individual tests.
*   **Scope:** This is used to run the same test logic multiple times with different data inputs (e.g., different names or expected values) within a single test file.

**Project-level parameterization**
*   **Implementation:** You define custom options in your test file using `base.test.extend` and then override those options within the `projects` array in your `playwright.config.ts` file.
*   **Scope:** This is used to run groups of tests with different configurations, such as different environments (e.g., staging vs. production), different timeouts, or different retry counts.

To differentiate tests across environments specifically, you can use the `projects` configuration in `playwright.config.ts` to set environment-specific values like `baseURL`. Additionally, if you are running tests across multiple environments and need to merge reports, you can use the `testConfig.tag` property to label tests with the environment name.

When Playwright Test is used to test web components, tests run in Node.js, while components run in the real browser. ## Different environments​ {#different-environments}

Evaluated scripts run in the browser environment, while your test runs in a testing environments. This means you cannot use variables from your test in the page and vice versa. Instead, you should pass them explicitly as an argument.

The following snippet is
WRONG
because it uses the variable directly:


`constdata='some data';constresult=awaitpage.evaluate(()=>{// WRONG: there is no "data" in the web page.window.myApp.use(data);});`


The following snippet is
CORRECT
because it passes the value explicitly as an argument:


`constdata='some data';// Pass |data| as a parameter.constresult=awaitpage.evaluate(data=>{window.myApp.use(data);},data);`

# Timeouts | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-timeouts>

## Test timeout​ {#test-timeout}

Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and
`beforeEach`
hooks is included in the test timeout.

Timed out test produces the following error:


`example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test ===========================Timeout of 30000ms exceeded.`


Additional separate timeout, of the same value, is shared between fixture teardowns and
`afterEach`
hooks, after the test function has finished.

The same timeout value also applies to
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
hooks, but they do not share time with any test.

### Set test timeout in the config​ {#set-test-timeout-in-the-config}

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({timeout:120_000,});`


API reference:
testConfig.timeout (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-timeout)
.

## Fixture timeout​ {#fixture-timeout}

By default,
fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures)
shares timeout with the test. However, for slow fixtures, especially
worker-scoped (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#worker-scoped-fixtures)
ones, it is convenient to have a separate timeout. This way you can keep the overall test timeout small, and give the slow fixture more time.

example.spec.ts

`import{testasbase,expect}from'@playwright/test';consttest=base.extend<{slowFixture:string}>({slowFixture:[async({},use)=>{// ... perform a slow operation ...awaituse('hello');},{timeout:60_000}]});test('example test',async({slowFixture})=>{// ...});`


API reference:
test.extend() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-extend)
.

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({use:{actionTimeout:10*1000,navigationTimeout:30*1000,},});`


API reference:
testOptions.actionTimeout (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testoptions#test-options-action-timeout)
and
testOptions.navigationTimeout (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testoptions#test-options-navigation-timeout)
.

### Set timeout for a single action​ {#set-timeout-for-a-single-action}

example.spec.ts

`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('basic test',async({page})=>{awaitpage.goto('https://playwright.dev',{timeout:30000});awaitpage.getByText('Get Started').click({timeout:10000});});`


## Fixture timeout​ {#fixture-timeout}

## Fixture timeout​ {#fixture-timeout}

Fixture is considered to be a part of a test, and so its setup and teardown running time counts towards the test timeout. Therefore, a slow fixture may cause test timeouts. You can set a separate larger timeout for such a fixture, and keep the overall test timeout small.


`import{testasbase,expect}from'@playwright/test';consttest=base.extend<{slowFixture:string}>({slowFixture:[async({},use)=>{// ... perform a slow operation ...awaituse('hello');},{timeout:60000}]});test('example test',async({slowFixture})=>{// ...});`

The test is not wrong, and CI is not wrong; the behavior is expected when a golden file does not yet exist.

When `await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()` is executed for the first time, the test runner generates the reference screenshot and reports the error you observed because there is no golden file yet. The runner saves the actual screenshot to the file system, and it is now ready to be added to the repository.

The reason the test passes locally but fails on CI is due to differences in the environment. Browser rendering can vary based on the host OS, version, settings, hardware, and other factors. Because the snapshot name includes the platform (e.g., `chromium-darwin`), Playwright requires different snapshots for different environments. To ensure consistent screenshots, you must run tests in the same environment where the baseline screenshots were generated.

## Strictness​ {#strictness}

Locators are strict. This means that all operations on locators that imply some target DOM element will throw an exception if more than one element matches. For example, the following call throws if there are several buttons in the DOM:

#### Throws an error if more than one​ {#throws-an-error-if-more-than-one}


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').click();`


On the other hand, Playwright understands when you perform a multiple-element operation, so the following call works perfectly fine when the locator resolves to multiple elements.

#### Works fine with multiple elements​ {#works-fine-with-multiple-elements}


`awaitpage.getByRole('button').count();`

reference: Only targeted input actions (click, fill, inputValue, etc.) retarget from label to control. Other methods, like expect(locator).toHaveText(), target the label itself and assert the label's text content, not the input field. This behavior is expected.
reference_contexts: Targeted input actions in Playwright automatically distinguish between labels and controls, so you can target the label to perform an action on the associated control.

However, other methods will target the label itself, for example expect(locator).toHaveText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-text) will assert the text content of the label, not the input field.

// Fill the input by targeting the label.

llm_response:
The `fill` method automatically resolves to the associated control when targeting a `<label>` element [2, 3, 5]. However, `toHaveText` asserts on the text content of the element selected by the locator itself. When you use `page.locator('label')`, you are selecting the label element, not the input field, so the assertion checks the label's text ("Password") rather than the input's value.

To assert on the value of the input field, you should target the input directly using `getByLabel` or `locator` and use `toHaveValue` instead of `toHaveText`.

**Recommended approach:**
Use `getByLabel` to target the input field associated with the label, then use `toHaveValue` to assert on the typed content:

```javascript
await expect(page.getByLabel('Password')).toHaveValue('your-password-value');
```

As shown in the documentation, `getByLabel` is the preferred way to locate form controls by their associated label [4, 6]. If you need to retrieve the value programmatically for other purposes, you can use `locator.inputValue()` [1].

llm_response:
To trigger the `dragover` event in all browsers, you need at least two mouse moves. Your current code only performs one hover on the drop element.

You should repeat the `locator.hover()` call on the drop element a second time before releasing the mouse. The correct sequence is:

1. `await page.locator('#item-to-be-dragged').hover();`
2. `await page.mouse.down();`
3. `await page.locator('#item-to-drop-at').hover();`
4. `await page.locator('#item-to-drop-at').hover();` (Second hover)
5. `await page.mouse.up();`

Alternatively, the documentation recommends using `locator.dragTo()` for drag-and-drop operations, as it handles these steps automatically.

## Modify API responses​ {#modify-api-responses}

Sometimes, it is essential to make an API request, but the response needs to be patched to allow for reproducible testing. In that case, instead of mocking the request, one can perform the request and fulfill it with the modified response.

# Mock APIs | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/mock>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Web APIs are usually implemented as HTTP endpoints. Playwright provides APIs to
mock
and
modify
network traffic, both HTTP and HTTPS. Any requests that a page does, including
XHRs (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest)
and
fetch (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API)
requests, can be tracked, modified and mocked. With Playwright you can also mock using HAR files that contain multiple network requests made by the page.

## Mock API requests​ {#mock-api-requests}

The following code will intercept all the calls to
`*/**/api/v1/fruits`
and will return a custom response instead. No requests to the API will be made. The test goes to the URL that uses the mocked route and asserts that mock data is present on the page.

In the example below we intercept the call to the fruit API and add a new fruit called 'Loquat', to the data. We then go to the url and assert that this data is there:


`test('gets the json from api and adds a new fruit',async({page})=>{// Get the response and add to itawaitpage.route('*/**/api/v1/fruits',asyncroute=>{constresponse=awaitroute.fetch();constjson=awaitresponse.json();json.push({name:'Loquat',id:100});// Fulfill using the original response, while patching the response body// with the given JSON object.awaitroute.fulfill({response,json});});// Go to the pageawaitpage.goto('https://demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking');// Assert that the new fruit is visibleawaitexpect(page.getByText('Loquat',{exact:true})).toBeVisible();});`


In the trace of our test we can see that the API was called and the response was modified.

By inspecting the response we can see that our new fruit was added to the list.

Read more about
advanced networking (https://playwright.dev/docs/network)
.

You can mock API endpoints via handling the network requests in your Playwright script.

#### Variations​ {#variations-1}

Set up route on the entire browser context with
browserContext.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-route)
or page with
page.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-route)
. It will apply to popup windows and opened links.


`awaitbrowserContext.route('**/api/login',route=>route.fulfill({status:200,body:'accept',}));awaitpage.goto('https://example.com');`


## Modify requests​ {#modify-requests}


`// Delete headerawaitpage.route('**/*',asyncroute=>{constheaders=route.request().headers();deleteheaders['X-Secret'];awaitroute.continue({headers});});// Continue requests as POST.awaitpage.route('**/*',route=>route.continue({method:'POST'}));`


You can continue requests with modifications. Example above removes an HTTP header from the outgoing requests.

## Abort requests​ {#abort-requests}

It might be that you are using a mock tool such as Mock Service Worker (MSW). While this tool works out of the box for mocking responses, it adds its own Service Worker that takes over the network requests, hence making them invisible to
browserContext.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-route)
and
page.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-route)
. If you are interested in both network testing and mocking, consider using built-in
browserContext.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-route)
and
page.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-route)
for
response mocking (https://playwright.dev/docs/network#handle-requests)
.

You can teardown your setup by adding a

First we add the

property to our setup project with the name 'cleanup db' which is the name we gave to our teardown project in the previous step:

user_input: A test keeps flaking on CI and I can't reproduce it locally. I want a way to see exactly what happened when it failed, without slowing down the whole run. What should I enable?
reference: Enable tracing on the first retry (trace: 'on-first-retry' with retries enabled). This produces a trace.zip for retried tests that you can open in Trace Viewer to explore each action, DOM snapshots, console and network. Traces are great for debugging failures on CI.
