llm_response:
To see exactly what happened when a test fails without slowing down the whole run, you should enable tracing on retries.

In your `playwright.config.ts` file, set the `trace` option to `'on-first-retry'`:

```javascript
use: {
  trace: 'on-first-retry',
},
```

This configuration collects a trace only when a test is retried after a failure, which avoids the overhead of recording traces for every test run. You can then view the trace, which includes action snapshots, logs, and source code locations, by opening the HTML report using `npx playwright show-report`.

Alternatively, if you do not enable retries but still want traces for failed tests, you can use `trace: 'retain-on-failure'`.

user_input: I want to run the exact same tests in two states — logged in and logged out — without duplicating the test code. What's a clean way to structure this?
reference: Reach for projects: they point the identical test files at more than one configuration — say one project with a signed-in storageState and one without — so you exercise both states without duplicating any test code.
reference_contexts: We use projects so we can run tests on different browsers and devices. Projects are configured in the playwright.config.ts file and once configured you can then run your tests on all projects or only on a specific project. llm_response:
To run tests in both logged-in and logged-out states without duplicating code, you can use the recommended approach of authenticating once in a setup project and reusing the authentication state.

### Recommended Approach: Setup Project
The documentation recommends authenticating once in a **setup project**, saving the authentication state, and then reusing it to bootstrap tests that require an authenticated state [7].

1.  **Generate and Save State:** Perform your authentication steps and save the storage state (cookies, `localStorage`, and `IndexedDB`) to a file, such as `auth.json` [1].
2.  **Reuse State:** You can consume this file in your tests to restore the authenticated state [1].
3.  **Security:** Because the state file contains sensitive information, you must add it to your `.gitignore` or delete it after use [1, 7].

### Alternative: Worker-Scoped Fixtures
If you need to handle authentication dynamically within your test suite, you can extend the base test to create a **worker-scoped fixture** [4, 6]. This allows you to:
*   Use `test.info().parallelIndex` to create unique authentication files for different workers [4, 6].
*   Check if a file exists to reuse authentication state [4, 6].
*   Authenticate in a clean environment by setting `storageState: undefined` when creating a new context or page [4, 6].

### Running Tests
*   **Logged-in:** You can run tests with the `--load-storage` flag to consume the saved `auth.json` [1].
*   **Logged-out:** By default, tests start from scratch (no storage state), which provides the necessary isolation to run tests without authentication [3].

By structuring your tests to use these fixtures or setup projects, you can maintain a single set of test code that executes in different states based on the configuration provided to the test runner.

reference: Pin the clock rather than trying to write assertions that hold at any hour. The recommended tool is page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00')), which fixes what Date.now() and new Date() return so the greeting and the relative timestamps render the same way on every run. reference_contexts: setFixedTime: Sets the fixed time for Date.now() and new Date().

The recommended approach is to use setFixedTime to set the time to a specific value. If that doesn't work for your use case, you can use install which allows you to pause time later on, fast forward it, tick it, etc. setSystemTime is only recommended for advanced use cases.

To make the page's idea of time deterministic, you should use `page.clock` to override native global time-related functions and manually control the passage of time.

The recommended approach is to use `page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('...'))` to set the time to a specific value.

If your use case requires more complex control, such as pausing time, fast-forwarding, or ticking through time, you should use `page.clock.install()`:

*   **To initialize and pause at a specific time:** Use `await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2024-02-02T08:00:00') });` followed by `await page.clock.pauseAt(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00'));`.
*   **To move time forward:** Use `await page.clock.fastForward('30:00');` to jump forward by a specific duration, or `await page.clock.runFor(2000);` to tick forward by a specific number of milliseconds, which fires all timers and animation frames in the process.

`page.clock` overrides native global classes and functions including `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `requestAnimationFrame`. Note that `setSystemTime` is only recommended for advanced use cases.

user_input: Tests running on different parallel workers keep colliding on the same database user. I want each worker to use its own isolated user. What's the recommended approach?
reference: Use a worker-scoped fixture keyed on testInfo.workerIndex (or process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX) to create a unique DB user per worker, initialized once and cleaned up after. All tests run by that worker reuse the same user.
reference_contexts: You can leverage process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX or testInfo.workerIndex (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#test-info-worker-index) mentioned above to isolate user data in the database between tests running on different workers. All tests run by the worker reuse the same user.
llm_response:
The recommended approach for tests that modify server-side state is to use one account per parallel worker. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once, and all tests run by that worker reuse the same authentication state.

To implement this:

1.  **Create a fixture:** Create a `playwright/fixtures.ts` file.
2.  **Differentiate workers:** Use `testInfo.parallelIndex` (or `process.env.TEST_PARALLEL_INDEX`) to differentiate between workers and ensure each is assigned a unique account.
3.  **Override storageState:** Override the `storageState` fixture in your `playwright/fixtures.ts` file to perform the authentication once per worker process.

Alternatively, if you are isolating user data in the database rather than using `storageState`, you can create a `dbUserName` fixture in `playwright/fixtures.ts` that uses `testInfo.workerIndex` to initialize a new user in the test database for each worker.

## Worker processes​ {#worker-processes}

All tests run in worker processes. These processes are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)

user_input: My CSS selectors keep breaking every time the DOM changes. I want locators that survive refactors. What should I use instead?
reference: Prefer user-facing locators like role and text (getByRole, getByText) or an explicit test id contract (getByTestId) instead of CSS/XPath, which are tied to implementation and break when the DOM changes.
reference_contexts: CSS and XPath are not recommended as the DOM can often change leading to non resilient tests. Instead, try to come up with a locator that is close to how the user perceives the page such as role locators or define an explicit testing contract using test ids.
Testing by test ids is the most resilient way of testing as even if your text or role of the attribute changes, the test will still pass.
llm_response:
To create resilient tests that survive refactors, you should avoid CSS and XPath selectors, as they are tied to the DOM structure and implementation. Instead, use the following approaches:

*   **User-visible locators (Recommended):** Prioritize locators that reflect how a user perceives the page, such as role locators (`page.getByRole()`) or text locators (`page.getByText()`).
*   **Explicit testing contracts:** Define test IDs to create a stable contract between your code and your tests (e.g., `page.locator('data-test-id=submit')`).

When you need to narrow down your selection, use `locator.filter()` to target elements based on their content or role, rather than relying on DOM structure.

## Fixture timeout​ {#fixture-timeout}

Fixture is considered to be a part of a test, and so its setup and teardown running time counts towards the test timeout. Therefore, a slow fixture may cause test timeouts. You can set a separate larger timeout for such a fixture, and keep the overall test timeout small.

user_input: I keep writing teardown code to clear cookies and local storage so one spec doesn't poison the next, and it still isn't enough — things like already-visited link styling survive anyway, and a test that fails halfway never gets to its cleanup. I'd rather every test just began from nothing.
reference: That's the default, and cleaning up between tests is the strategy the docs advise against — it's easy to forget, and some state (visited links being the standard example) simply cannot be cleaned up, so leakage shows up later as a confusing failure in a different test. The alternative is to start from scratch, which is what browser contexts give you: each test gets its own BrowserContext, an incognito-like profile with its own cookies, local storage and session storage, created fresh for that test and completely isolated even when several run in one browser. With the test runner this happens automatically — the `page` and `context` fixtures in each test belong to a context created for it — so you can delete the teardown rather than fix it. Contexts are cheap and fast to create, so there's no cost argument for reusing one.
reference_contexts: Tests written with Playwright execute in isolated clean-slate environments called browser contexts. This isolation model improves reproducibility and prevents cascading test failures.

Test Isolation is when each test is completely isolated from another test. Every test runs independently from any other test. This means that each test has its own local storage, session storage, cookies etc. Playwright achieves this using BrowserContexts which are equivalent to incognito-like profiles. They are fast and cheap to create and are completely isolated, even when running in a single browser.

There are two different strategies when it comes to Test Isolation: start from scratch or cleanup in between. The problem with cleaning up in between tests is that it can be easy to forget to clean up and some things are impossible to clean up such as "visited links".
Playwright uses browser contexts to achieve Test Isolation. Each test has its own Browser Context. Running the test creates a new browser context each time.
llm_response: To ensure every test begins from nothing, you should adopt the "start from scratch" strategy for test isolation. The documentation notes that "cleanup in between tests" is problematic because it is easy to forget to clean up, and certain states, such as "visited links," are impossible to clean up. Starting from scratch ensures that everything is new, which also simplifies debugging because you only need to look within the failing test itself.

user_input: I run sharded tests as separate CI jobs and end up with a separate report per shard. I want one combined report at the end. What's the workflow?

llm_response:
To produce a combined report from sharded CI jobs, follow these steps:

1.  **Configure the Blob Reporter:** Update your `playwright.config.ts` to use the `blob` reporter when running in CI:
    ```typescript
    export default defineConfig({
      testDir: './tests',
      reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',
    });
    ```
    The blob reporter generates `.zip` files containing the test run data.

2.  **Run Sharded Tests:** Configure your CI jobs to run tests using the `--shard=x/y` flag. For example, using a GitHub Actions matrix:
    *   Set `shardTotal` to the total number of shards.
    *   Set `shardIndex` to the specific shard number.
    *   Run the command: `npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }}`.
    *   Upload the resulting blob reports to GitHub Actions Artifacts.

3.  **Merge Reports:** Create a separate job in your workflow that runs after the test jobs (using `needs: [playwright-tests]`). In this job:
    *   Download all blob reports from the artifacts into a single directory (e.g., `./all-blob-reports`).
    *   Run the merge command:
        `npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports`
    *   This produces a standard HTML report in the `playwright-report` directory, which you can then upload as an artifact.
llm_references:

With

Without

To ensure the most effective use of sharding, especially in CI environments, it is recommended to use
`fullyParallel: true`
when aiming for balanced distribution across shards. Otherwise, you may need to manually organize your test files to avoid imbalances.

In the previous example, each test shard has its own test report. If you want to have a combined report showing all the test results from all the shards, you can merge them.

`blob`

playwright.config.ts

`exportdefaultdefineConfig({testDir:'./tests',reporter:process.env.CI?'blob':'html',});`

`npx playwright merge-reports--reporterhtml ./all-blob-reports`


This will produce a standard HTML report into
`playwright-report`
directory.

## GitHub Actions example​ {#github-actions-example}

GitHub Actions supports
sharding tests between multiple jobs (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-jobs/using-a-matrix-for-your-jobs)
using the
jobs.<job_id>.strategy.matrix (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions#jobsjob_idstrategymatrix)
option. The
`matrix`
option will run a separate job for every possible combination of the provided options.

The following example shows you how to configure a job to run your tests on four machines in parallel and then merge the reports into a single report. Don't forget to add
`reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',`
to your
`playwright.config.ts`
file as in the example above.

First we add a
`matrix`
option to our job configuration with the
`shardTotal: [4]`
option containing the total number of shards we want to create and
`shardIndex: [1, 2, 3, 4]`
with an array of the shard numbers.
Then we run our Playwright tests with the
`--shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }}`
option. This will run our test command for each shard.
Finally we upload our blob report to the GitHub Actions Artifacts. This will make the blob report available to other jobs in the workflow.

This is the

modify server-side state
. In Playwright, worker processes run in parallel. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once. All tests ran by worker are reusing the same authentication state. We will need multiple testing accounts, one per each parallel worker.

When to use

Your tests modify shared server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting.

When not to use

Your tests do not modify any shared server-side state. In this case, all tests can use a single shared account.

Details
